title: Traditional Schools Are Losing Their Grip on K-12 Education
author: Ray Domanico
summary: Ray Domanico reviews Mickey Revenaugh's book School's Out, which argues that deep social, cultural and technological forces are driving the growth of homeschooling, microschools and other unconventional education. He notes that although only about 2 percent of students are in these settings, the families involved have rejected the self-contained school and assembled an a la carte mix of virtual learning, pods, microschools and community resources. Customization lets parents match pace to a child's ability, follow interests in arts and music, and count museums, apprenticeships and nature programs as real learning. The review highlights the growing diversity of these families, including a sharp rise in Black homeschooling, and links it to frustration with district equity programs where adult interests overtake children's. It also records Revenaugh's honest concern about the cloche effect of small like-minded groups. Domanico concludes that school choice, AI and work-from-home policy are changing the relationship between families and schools, so that the standardized program is losing its grip.
points: Families using alternative education build customized programs from virtual learning, pods, microschools and community resources, rejecting the self-contained school.
Customization lets parents match pace to the child's abilities, follow interests peripheral in traditional schools, and treat real-world experiences as learning on par with books.
The growth of homeschooling among Black and Hispanic families is tied to frustration with district programs where adult interests displace children's outcomes.
The book acknowledges real concerns about the cloche effect of small, like-minded learning communities, while noting that traditional schools are often segregated too.
School choice, AI and work-from-home flexibility together are loosening schools' role as sole intermediaries between families and educational technology.
quotes: Parents choosing these options have lost faith in the traditional school model, which places students in age-specific grades in a single physical space to learn a common curriculum.
They take an à la carte approach, mixing and matching virtual learning, learning pods (small-group settings), microschools, community resources, and other alternatives into a comprehensive program.
Fine-tuning the educational program allows parents to match the pace of learning to their child’s abilities, rather than to the dictates of the clock or calendar.
Over time, however, the interests of the adults in the classrooms take priority over those of the children, and money continues to flow into the programs despite a lack of progress.

Revenaugh discusses the possible drawbacks of self- and family-directed education, acknowledging “real concerns about the ‘cloche effect’ of very small, self-contained learning communities of like-minded families.

Parents now have the tools to design an educational program that suits their children. Schools and districts are no longer the sole intermediaries between families and educational technology, for better or worse.
The standardized program of traditional schools and districts is losing its grip on American families.
